Series::min¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::min() const -> Series
Series::min(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::min(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series
Series::min(const Series& other) const -> Series

Series::min_pair(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim = false) const
    -> std::pair<Series, Series>

What It Does¶

min() is the lower-bound companion to max(), and it has the same overload split:

  • reduction overloads answer “what is the smallest value?”

  • the binary overload answers “at each position, which input is smaller?”

That makes min() another method where the public name stays the same while the mental model changes with the overload family.

  • min() reduces the whole Series to one scalar winner

  • min(dim) and min(dim, keepdim) reduce one axis

  • min(other) performs an elementwise lower-of-two comparison under broadcasting

If you are learning to read the API fluently, it helps to separate “ordered reduction” from “pairwise comparison” every time you see this method.

Overload Map¶

min()

Reduces across the entire Series and returns one scalar minimum.

min(dim)

Reduces one axis and removes that axis from the output shape.

min(dim, keepdim)

Reduces one axis and optionally keeps it as size 1.

min(other)

Returns the elementwise smaller value between self and other under broadcasting. Forward values match minimum().

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis used by the reduction overloads.

  • positive dims count from the front

  • negative dims count from the back

  • the dim must refer to an existing axis

Changing the dim changes which values compete to become the minimum. On a rank-2 Series, dim = 0 compares within each column, while dim = 1 compares within each row.

keepdim (bool)

Controls shape retention for the reduced axis.

  • false: remove the axis

  • true: keep the axis as size 1

This toggle matters when the reduced output will be reused in shape-sensitive operations later on.

other (const Series&)

The peer Series for the binary overload.

  • other is broadcast against self

  • the result takes the broadcasted shape

  • no axis is reduced in this overload

So min(other) is best understood as a comparison surface, not as a special case of reduction.

Returns¶

Series The returned Series is:

- scalar for `min()`
- reduced for `min(dim, ...)`
- broadcasted for `min(other)`

Gradient¶

Like max(), min() has different backward behavior for reduction and binary comparison overloads.

Reduction Overloads¶

For min(), min(dim), and min(dim, keepdim):

  • only winning minima receive sensitivity

  • equal minima inside one reduced lane split the incoming derivative evenly

  • the full reduction overload splits across every global minimum in the whole Series

So reduction min(...) is tie-sharing.

Binary Overload¶

For min(other):

  • backward routing matches minimum()

  • gradient flows to self where self <= other

  • gradient flows to other where self > other

  • at an exact tie, the derivative stays with self

So the binary overload is again left-biased at the tie boundary.

Paired Value And Index (min_pair)¶

min_pair(dim [, keepdim]) runs the axis reduction and returns both channels at once: .first is the winning values (identical to min(dim, keepdim)), .second is the int64 position each winner held along dim (identical to argmin(dim, keepdim)). The result is a std::pair<Series, Series> – result.first is the values, result.second the indices.

Use it when you need the smallest value and where it sits without two separate scans. There is no whole-series overload — min_pair always reduces a named axis. On a tie inside a lane the reported index is the first occurrence, matching argmin(). The value channel is differentiable exactly as min(dim) is; the index channel never carries gradient.

Examples¶

The examples below build from the simplest scalar reduction through axis-aware reductions, then on to broadcasting, gradient behavior, and failure modes.

Example 1. min() with no arguments returns the single smallest value in the whole Series.

auto lows = pluss::make_series({
    {4.0, 1.0, 3.0},
    {2.0, 1.0, 6.0},
});

std::cout << lows.min();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1

This is a scalar Series, so the entire input has been reduced to one global winner.

Example 2. min(0) reduces down columns.

std::cout << lows.min(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 1, 3]

Each column contributes one minimum, which is why the result shape is [3].

Example 3. min(1) reduces across columns within each row.

std::cout << lows.min(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

Now the shape is [2] because each row contributes one winner.

Example 4. keepdim=true keeps the reduced axis available as size 1.

std::cout << lows.min(1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[1],
  [1]]

The values are unchanged from Example 3. Only the shape policy changed.

Example 5. Negative dims count from the back.

std::cout << lows.min(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

For this rank-2 input, -1 means the last axis, so this matches min(1).

Example 6. min(other) is an elementwise comparison under broadcasting.

auto ceilings = pluss::make_series({3.0, 2.0, 4.0});

std::cout << lows.min(ceilings);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[3, 1, 3],
  [2, 1, 4]]

The right-hand input is broadcast across rows, and each position keeps the smaller contender.

Example 7. min(other) and minimum(other) have the same forward values.

std::cout << lows.minimum(ceilings);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[3, 1, 3],
  [2, 1, 4]]

This is a helpful equivalence because it shows that the binary overload belongs to the elementwise comparison family, not the reduction family.

Example 8. On an axis reduction, tied minima split the derivative evenly.

auto reduced_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {2.0, 1.0, 1.0},
    {3.0, -4.0, -4.0},
});
reduced_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto reduced_winners = reduced_ties.min(1);
reduced_winners.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << reduced_winners << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << reduced_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, -4]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0.5, 0.5],
  [0, 0.5, 0.5]]

Each row has two equal minima, so each winner receives half of that row’s upstream sensitivity.

Example 9. Full reduction splits the derivative across every global minimum in the entire Series.

auto global_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {-5.0, 0.0, 0.0},
    {-5.0, -5.0, 1.0},
});
global_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto global_winner = global_ties.min();
global_winner.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << global_winner << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << global_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-5
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.33333333, 0, 0],
  [0.33333333, 0.33333333, 0]]

There are three global minima, so each one receives one third of the upstream sensitivity.

Example 10. The binary overload does not split ties. At equal values, the left operand keeps the gradient.

auto lhs = pluss::make_series({1.0, 5.0, 2.0});
auto rhs = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 2.0});
lhs.tracks_slope_(true);
rhs.tracks_slope_(true);

auto binary = lhs.min(rhs);
binary.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << binary << "\n";
std::cout << "dlhs=" << lhs.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "drhs=" << rhs.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 2]
dlhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 1]
drhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 0]

Positions 0 and 2 tie, and both gradients stay with lhs. That is the main backward quirk to remember for the binary overload.

Example 11. A reduction dim must refer to a real axis.

try {
  std::cout << lows.min(2) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

This is the expected failure mode when the dim does not exist.

Example 12. min_pair(dim) returns the smallest values and their positions together.

auto grid = pluss::make_series({
    {3.0, 1.0, 4.0},
    {1.0, 5.0, 9.0},
});

auto result = grid.min_pair(1);
std::cout << "values=" << result.first << "\n";
std::cout << "indices=" << result.second;

Output¶

values=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]
indices=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0]

Row 0’s smallest value is 1 at column 1; row 1’s is 1 at column 0.

Example 13. The value channel of min_pair is differentiable; the index channel is inert.

auto grid = pluss::make_series({
    {3.0, 1.0, 4.0},
    {1.0, 5.0, 9.0},
});
grid.tracks_slope_(true);

grid.min_pair(1).first.sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, grid.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 0.0000 1.0000 0.0000 ⎤
⎣ 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000 ⎦

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • min() and min(other) are different operation families that happen to share a name.

  • dim = 0 and dim = 1 compare different lanes and usually produce different shapes.

  • keepdim=true preserves the reduced axis but does not change which values win.

  • Reduction overloads split ties evenly; binary min(other) sends tie gradients to the left operand.

  • Broadcastability matters for min(other).

  • Out-of-range dims throw immediately.

  • min_pair has no whole-series overload — it always takes a dim. Its index channel reports the first tied position and never carries gradient.

Summary¶

Use min() when you need the smallest value itself.

  • Choose min() for one global minimum.

  • Choose min(dim) when each axis lane should contribute its own local minimum.

  • Choose keepdim=true when you need the reduced result to stay easy to align with the original shape.

  • Choose min(other) when the task is elementwise lower-of-two selection under broadcasting.

Once that overload choice is clear, the rest follows naturally: reductions change shape and share ties, while pairwise comparison preserves a broadcasted shape and keeps tie gradients on the left operand.

See Also¶

  • Series::minimum: explicit elementwise minimum surface.

  • Series::max: upper-bound counterpart with the same overload map.

  • Series::argmin: returns winning indices instead of winning values.

  • Series::max / Series::argmax: the upper-bound counterparts, including max_pair.
